talks.title: Library 4 Pairing-based TransformCrypto
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### Introduction to Pairing-Based Cryptography
At 00:00, Bob Wall and Colt Frederickson introduce an open-source cryptographic library designed to make pairing-based cryptography and proxy re-encryption practical for enterprise software engineering.

### Mathematical Mechanics of Proxy Re-Encryption
At 09:00, the speakers explain proxy re-encryption (PRE). The protocol allows a semi-trusted third party (such as a cloud storage server) to transform ciphertext encrypted under Alice's public key into ciphertext that can be decrypted by Bob's private key, without the proxy ever seeing the plaintext data or private keys.

### Implementing Bilinear Pairings on Elliptic Curves
At 18:02, the presenters delve into the underlying mathematics, discussing bilinear pairings (such as Tate and Weil pairings) constructed over specialized elliptic curves. They detail how these mathematical structures enable non-interactive access delegation, identity-based encryption (IBE), and fine-grained access control policies.

### Enterprise Access Delegation and Offboarding Workflows
At 27:04, Wall and Frederickson demonstrate practical enterprise applications. In multi-user cloud platforms, PRE enables dynamic data sharing—such as onboarding external contractors or medical specialists—without requiring the original data owner to repeatedly decrypt and re-encrypt files.

### Crypto-Shredding and Revocation Architecture
Concluding at 36:00, the authors address key revocation and "crypto-shredding." By securely discarding or invalidating re-encryption keys stored on the proxy, access to massive historical datasets is cryptographically severed instantly, eliminating the need to physically delete multi-terabyte files from distributed storage.

talks.title: Cryptography Codes and Secret Writing
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### Historical Fundamentals of Cryptography and Ciphers
At 00:00, Tess Schrodinger opens an educational survey of classical ciphers and modern cryptography at the Crypto and Privacy Village. Schrodinger introduces foundational terminology, distinguishing between encoding, steganography, and mathematical encryption.

### Hash Functions: One-Way Primitives and Collision Resistance
At 18:11, Schrodinger breaks down the mathematical properties of cryptographic hash functions. She demonstrates the avalanche effect, explaining why minor modifications to input data drastically alter resulting digests, and compares legacy algorithms like MD5 and SHA-1 to modern standards like SHA-256.

### Classical Cryptanalysis and Frequency Analysis
At 38:30, the presentation covers pen-and-paper cipher systems, including Caesar, substitution, and Vigenère polyalphabetic ciphers. Schrodinger demonstrates how frequency analysis—evaluating letter distributions and English language characteristics—allows cryptanalysts to break classical ciphers without knowing the key.

### Asymmetric Cryptography and Public-Key Infrastructure
At 58:13, the talk transitions to modern asymmetric encryption. Schrodinger explains the mathematical mechanics behind RSA and Diffie-Hellman key exchanges, contrasting symmetric shared-secret ciphers with public-private keypairs.

### Future Horizons: Quantum Key Distribution
Concluding between 01:05:00 and 01:15:00, Schrodinger introduces quantum cryptography. She explains how quantum key distribution (QKD) leverages photon polarization and Heisenberg's uncertainty principle to detect eavesdropping, preparing attendees for post-quantum cryptographic challenges.

talks.title: Reyes, Elazari, On Wont Somebody Think of the Children
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### Large-Scale Privacy Analysis of Children's Mobile Apps
At 00:00, computer science researcher Irwin Reyes and cybersecurity legal scholar Amit Elazari open an empirical investigation into Children's Online Privacy Protection Act (COPPA) compliance across the modern mobile application ecosystem.

### Automated Dynamic Testing at Massive Scale
At 04:02, Reyes outlines the testing methodology, which analyzed approximately 80,000 Android applications directed at children. Using automated dynamic analysis sandboxes, the researchers monitored runtime memory, API calls, and outbound network traffic to observe actual data exfiltration in real time.

### Statutory Requirements and FTC Enforcement History
At 08:02, Elazari reviews the statutory architecture of COPPA and Federal Trade Commission (FTC) enforcement trends. COPPA strictly prohibits collecting persistent identifiers from children under thirteen without verified parental consent, yet violations remain widespread across popular consumer apps.

### Third-Party Ad Networks and SDK Non-Compliance
At 12:01, the presenters expose systemic tracking by third-party advertising and analytics SDKs. Even when software development kits explicitly forbid integration into child-directed apps in their terms of service, hundreds of mobile games routinely bundled these SDKs to harvest Android Advertising IDs, MAC addresses, and geolocation data.

### Auditing Safe Harbor Certification Programs
Concluding between 16:01 and 20:01, the speakers deliver a critique of FTC-approved "Safe Harbor" certification programs. The empirical data reveals that apps displaying certified privacy seals frequently violated COPPA at rates comparable to uncertified applications, demonstrating significant oversight gaps in self-regulatory privacy regimes.

talks.title: Jailed by a Google Search
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### The Weaponization of Search Surveillance
At 00:00, digital rights researcher Pigeon delivers a presentation on the surveillance of reproductive healthcare at the Crypto and Privacy Village. Pigeon details how law enforcement agencies utilize digital footprints to investigate and prosecute self-induced healthcare decisions.

### Subpoenaing Personal Search Queries and Pharmacy Visits
At 04:43, the presentation reviews case studies where criminal prosecutions relied on corporate search logs and digital browsing histories. Pigeon recounts instances where search engine queries for medication dosages and digital receipts from online pharmacies were subpoenaed and used as courtroom evidence.

### Geofence Warrants, Reverse Search Warrants, and Wi-Fi Sniffing
At 09:21, Pigeon explains law enforcement surveillance mechanisms including geofence warrants and reverse keyword searches. She highlights how wardriving databases (such as WiGLE) and cellular location telemetry enable dragnet identification of individuals visiting medical clinics.

### Expanding Legal Surveillance Frameworks
At 13:54, the speaker examines historical and pending federal communications legislation. She warns that statutes regulating digital telecommunications could be repurposed to criminalize the transmission of reproductive health information and encryption technologies across state lines.

### Operational Security Countermeasures for Personal Privacy
Concluding between 15:00 and 18:12, Pigeon provides concrete operational security advice for vulnerable individuals. She recommends using the Tor browser, burner hardware, encrypted messaging applications like Signal, and disabling location services to prevent algorithmic tracking.

talks.title: Hiding in plain sight Disguising HTTPS traffic
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### Passive Inspection and TLS Metadata Leakage
At 00:00, network researcher Matt Urquhart examines the vulnerabilities of encrypted communications, exploring techniques for disguising HTTPS traffic to evade passive network monitoring and deep packet inspection (DPI).

### Plaintext Indicators in Encrypted Handshakes
At 07:00, Urquhart explains how conventional HTTPS connections leak destinations. Even though payload data is encrypted, the initial TLS ClientHello packet contains the Server Name Indication (SNI) extension in cleartext, while unencrypted DNS queries expose the destination domain to internet service providers and intermediate firewalls.

### Domain Fronting Architecture on Cloud CDNs
At 14:01, the speaker explores domain fronting over multi-tenant content delivery networks (CDNs) like CloudFront and Google Cloud. By setting the outer TLS SNI to an innocuous, high-reputation domain while embedding the true, restricted destination within the encrypted HTTP Host header, traffic traverses perimeters without revealing the actual target.

### Traffic Fingerprinting and Flow Analysis
At 21:00, Urquhart reviews DPI fingerprinting heuristics. Network surveillance appliances analyze packet length sequences, packet timing intervals, and TCP window adjustments to fingerprint specific protocols and identify domain fronting activity even when SNI matches known domains.

### Packet Fragmentation and SNI Disguise
Concluding between 28:00 and 35:00, Urquhart demonstrates transport-layer obfuscation. By splitting the TLS ClientHello packet across TCP segment boundaries or injecting benign out-of-order packets, the sender disrupts deep packet inspection parsers, allowing privacy-preserving communications through restrictive network environments.

talks.title: Prototyping Cryptographic Protocols
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### Rapid Prototyping with the Charm Cryptography Framework
At 00:00, Matt Cheung presents a guide to prototyping cryptographic protocols using Python and the Charm-Crypto library at the Crypto and Privacy Village. Cheung discusses how high-level language bindings streamline the development and evaluation of complex mathematical protocols.

### Bilinear Pairings and Identity-Based Encryption
At 14:22, Cheung walks through implementing Identity-Based Encryption (IBE) and pairing-based cryptography. He explains how Charm provides clean object-oriented abstractions over underlying C libraries (such as PBC and GMP), enabling developers to instantiate elliptic curve groups and evaluate bilinear maps in minimal lines of code.

### Interactive Zero-Knowledge Proofs in Python
At 26:13, the presentation covers zero-knowledge proofs, focusing on Sigma protocols and Schnorr identification schemes. Cheung demonstrates how developers can define cryptographic commitments, challenges, and mathematical responses, verifying that equations balance correctly across simulated network sockets.

### Protocol Optimization and Vector Search
At 36:49, Cheung explores practical protocol engineering challenges, including character delay vectors (CDV) and searchable encryption algorithms. He evaluates computational latency trade-offs between group exponentiations and network serialization overhead.

### Transitioning from Prototypes to Production Code
Concluding between 42:00 and 47:05, Cheung highlights the crucial distinction between research prototyping and production cryptography. He cautions that prototype code lacks side-channel defenses and constant-time execution guarantees, advising engineers to audit and port verified designs into memory-safe production languages.

talks.title: Rethinking Digital Privacy Education
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### Evaluating Digital Privacy Pedagogies for Youth
At 00:00, educational researchers Caroline Hardin and Jenn Dalsen present an empirical study examining digital privacy education, contrasting mainstream educational curricula with the lived experiences and threat models of modern youth.

### Surveying InfoSec Professionals and Educators
At 03:00, the authors outline their survey methodology, which polled cybersecurity professionals, computer science educators, and young adults to evaluate the practical efficacy of standard privacy lessons taught in secondary schools.

### Critiquing Victim-Blaming and Surveillance Paternalism
At 06:00 and 09:01, Hardin and Dalsen critique pervasive educational frameworks like "digital citizenship contracts" and "think before you post" campaigns. These curricula place the entire burden of privacy defense on young individuals while ignoring systemic data harvesting by advertising conglomerates and school monitoring software.

### Equity and Disproportionate Privacy Burdens
At 12:05, the presentation examines privacy through an equity lens. Low-income and marginalized youth often rely on school-issued laptops and free public Wi-Fi networks subject to invasive administrative surveillance, leaving them unable to adopt privacy advice tailored for affluent demographics with private devices.

### Constructing Participatory, Practical Privacy Curricula
Concluding around 15:00, the speakers demonstrate interactive privacy workshops. They advocate replacing paternalistic prohibitions with participatory curricula teaching threat modeling, ad-blocker configuration, tracker resistance, and setting healthy interpersonal communication boundaries.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Revolutionizing Auth with Oblivious Crypto
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### The Crisis of Centralized Credential Storage
At 00:00, Adam Everspaugh introduces oblivious pseudorandom functions (OPRF) and cryptographic authentication at the Crypto and Privacy Village. Everspaugh discusses how corporate credential breaches continue to expose hundreds of millions of user passwords despite standard hashing mechanisms.

### Limitations of Traditional Password Hashing
At 04:54, Everspaugh reviews traditional server-side hashing algorithms like bcrypt and Argon2. While these functions slow down guessing, attackers who breach database servers can still run massively parallelized offline dictionary attacks using GPU clusters without detection.

### Architecture of Oblivious Authentication
At 09:49, the speaker introduces OPRF-based authentication systems. Under this protocol, the client and an authentication server jointly evaluate a pseudorandom function: the client learns the cryptographic token without revealing their plaintext password, while the server evaluates the token without learning the user's secret.

### Blinded Cryptographic Evaluations and Mathematical Security
At 14:42, Everspaugh details the mathematical mechanisms behind blinded evaluation protocols. By utilizing elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman operations with blinding factors, the user masks their credentials before transmission, mathematically preventing the authentication server from logging or compromising user credentials.

### Rate Limiting and Protecting Against Data Breaches
Concluding between 21:35 and 26:44, Everspaugh presents Pythia, an OPRF-based password hardening architecture. By isolating rate limiting into specialized cryptographic key servers, service providers can enforce strict query thresholds, preventing offline dictionary attacks even if backend databases are completely leaked.

talks.title: Announcing the Underhanded Crypto Contest
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### Deceptive Cryptography and the Underhanded Contest
At 00:00, Adam Caudill and Taylor Hornby present the winning entries of the inaugural Underhanded Crypto Contest. The competition challenged developers to write seemingly correct, benign cryptographic code containing stealthy, deniable backdoors that evade automated analysis and human code audits.

### The Educational Value of Deceptive Code Auditing
At 02:01, the organizers explain the contest's defensive philosophy. By studying how adversaries construct subtle flaws with plausible deniability, security researchers and auditors can recognize deceptive design patterns in third-party libraries and national standards.

### Deconstructing the Podium Submissions
At 04:02 and 06:00, the presenters review the top entries. The third-place entry used a clever Bash script that covertly leaked private key material via environment variables, while the second-place entry targeted Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH) key exchange, manipulating scalar multiplication logic to force shared secrets into small, predictable subgroups.

### Asymmetric Backdoors in Elliptic Curve Parameter Selection
At 08:01 and 10:00, Caudill and Hornby analyze the first-place winning submission. The implementation exploited obscure mathematical properties in curve parameter selection, creating an asymmetric backdoor where only the author—possessing private mathematical constants—can decrypt communications while the library passes standard cryptographic unit tests.

### Defensive Imperatives: Parameter Scrutiny and Formal Proofs
Concluding the session, the authors emphasize that standard functional tests cannot detect intentional subversion. Ensuring cryptographic integrity requires rigorous parameter transparency, automated formal verification, and strict scrutiny of unusual mathematical shortcuts.

(AI summary — Gemini Flash)

talks.title: Anonymous Rate Limiting in Services
talks.teaser: Presentation on cryptography and privacy technologies.
talks.summary:
### Balancing Abuse Prevention with User Anonymity
At 00:00, Alex Catarineu and Konark Modi present an architecture for anonymous rate limiting using Direct Anonymous Attestation (DAA) at the Crypto and Privacy Village. The authors address the conflict between mitigating distributed denial-of-service (DoS) attacks and preserving user anonymity.

### Inadequacy of Traditional Identifier-Based Rate Limiting
At 04:48, the speakers explain that conventional rate-limiting architectures rely on tracking client IP addresses, cookies, or device fingerprints. In privacy-preserving ecosystems, persistent identifiers compromise user anonymity and allow service providers to build invasive browsing profiles.

### Direct Anonymous Attestation (DAA) Mechanics
At 09:56, Catarineu and Modi detail the mechanics of Direct Anonymous Attestation. DAA utilizes hardware security modules (such as Trusted Platform Modules) to create cryptographic group signatures, allowing a device to prove it belongs to an authorized group without disclosing its specific identity.

### Controlled Linkability and Epoch Base-Names
At 15:30, the talk explores controlled linkability. By incorporating structured base-names containing time epochs and request types, the system allows verifiers to link multiple requests originating from the same device within a short time window, enabling rate-limiting without uncovering long-term identity.

### Deployment Benchmarks and Client Implementations
Concluding between 21:18 and 27:39, the presenters share performance benchmarks and review open-source client-server implementations. They demonstrate that DAA rate-limiting provides scalable DoS protection suitable for production privacy networks.
